_: ARTICLES AND CASE. The biggest single category of beginner error, and the one where the wrong word is a real word, so nothing looks broken. Each entry states the rule first — the part that is also true next time — and never mentions a specific noun, because the same key fires on every sentence.

why: Masculine der becomes den in the accusative — the direct object of a verb. Only masculine changes; die, das and plural die look the same in the nominative and the accusative, which is why this one catches everybody.
This is the subject, so masculine stays der. den is for the direct object. The quick check: whoever or whatever is doing the verb is nominative.
Masculine der becomes dem in the dative — after mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu, aus, and as the indirect object (the person something is given to).
dem is masculine or neuter dative. Feminine dative is also der, which is the trap: die Frau becomes der Frau, not dem Frau.
den is accusative, dem is dative. Ask what the verb or preposition wants: mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu, aus always take the dative, whatever is happening.
This wants the accusative, so masculine is den. dem is dative — after mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu, aus, or for the person receiving something.
Feminine die becomes der in the dative and the genitive. It looks like the masculine nominative and it is not — this is the single most common article slip in German.
This noun is feminine, or it is a plural. Nouns ending in -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tion, -ei and -in are feminine without exception, which covers a lot of ground.
This noun is neuter. Reliable neuter endings: -chen, -lein, -ment, -um, and every verb used as a noun (das Essen, das Lernen).
Feminine, or plural. Every plural takes die in the nominative and the accusative, whatever the singular gender was.
This noun is masculine. Days, months, seasons, weather and points of the compass are masculine, as are most nouns ending in -er, -ling, -ismus and -or.
This noun is neuter. Learn the article with the word, never after it — the gender is not guessable from the meaning, only sometimes from the ending.
Neuter das becomes dem in the dative — after mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu, aus, and as the indirect object.
Neuter is das in both the nominative and the accusative. dem is the dative form, which this position does not want.
Plural dative is den, and the noun takes an extra -n as well: mit den Kindern, not mit die Kinder. It is the one plural form that changes.
Plural in the nominative and the accusative is die. den is plural dative, which needs a dative trigger.
The genitive shows possession: masculine and neuter take des, and the noun adds -s or -es. Spoken German mostly uses von dem instead, but writing keeps it.
Feminine and plural genitive is der, not des. des is only masculine and neuter.
Neuter genitive is des, and the noun adds -s or -es: des Kindes.
Masculine ein becomes einen in the accusative. The indefinite article follows exactly the same pattern as der/den — if you know one you know the other.
einen is masculine accusative. In the nominative — the subject — it is ein, and neuter is ein in both cases.
Masculine and neuter ein becomes einem in the dative: mit einem Freund, aus einem Haus.
einem is dative. Without a dative trigger — mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu, aus, or an indirect object — masculine and neuter are ein or einen.
Feminine eine becomes einer in the dative and the genitive, mirroring die → der.
Feminine is eine in both the nominative and the accusative. einer is the dative or genitive form.
eine is feminine; this noun is masculine or neuter, so it takes ein. There is no plural of ein — plural indefinite is simply no article at all.
This noun is feminine, so the indefinite article is eine.
einen is accusative, einem is dative. mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu and aus take the dative every time.
This is the direct object, so masculine takes einen. einem needs a dative trigger.
Masculine and neuter genitive is eines, and the noun adds -s or -es.
kein takes exactly the same endings as ein, so masculine accusative is keinen.
keinen is masculine accusative. The subject form is kein, and neuter is kein in both cases.
Masculine and neuter dative is keinem — same endings as ein, plus the plural form keinen that ein does not have.
Feminine dative is keiner, matching einer and der.
Feminine and plural take keine. This is where kein goes beyond ein: there is no plural ein, but there is a plural keine.
Masculine accusative is keinen. Feminine and plural stay keine — only masculine changes in the accusative.
This noun is masculine or neuter in a position that takes the bare form, so it is kein.
The possessives — mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer — all take ein's endings, so masculine accusative is meinen.
meinen is masculine accusative or plural dative. The subject form is mein.
Masculine and neuter dative is meinem: mit meinem Bruder.
Feminine dative is meiner: mit meiner Schwester.
Masculine accusative is meinen; plural dative is also meinen. Feminine and plural elsewhere stay meine.
dein takes ein's endings, so masculine accusative is deinen.
sein means his or its and takes ein's endings, so masculine accusative is seinen. Do not confuse it with the verb sein.
ihr means her or their and takes ein's endings, so masculine accusative is ihren.
unser takes ein's endings, so masculine accusative is unseren — often written unsern in speech, but unseren in writing.
dieser takes der's endings exactly, so masculine accusative is diesen, mirroring der → den.
diesen is masculine accusative. The subject form is dieser.
Masculine and neuter dative is diesem, mirroring der/das → dem.
Feminine dative is dieser, mirroring die → der.
Masculine accusative and plural dative are both diesen.
Neuter dative is diesem. dieses is the neuter nominative and accusative, and the masculine and neuter genitive.
welcher takes der's endings, so masculine accusative is welchen.
jeder takes der's endings, so masculine accusative is jeden — jeden Tag, every day, is the phrase you will meet it in most.
Masculine and neuter dative is jedem.
Plural dative is allen, and the noun adds -n too: mit allen Freunden.

_: PERFECT TENSE AUXILIARY. Choosing haben where sein is needed is the error that marks a learner out fastest, because it is so regular in German and so absent from English.

why: Verbs of movement from one place to another, and verbs of changing state, build the perfect with sein, not haben: er ist gegangen, gefahren, gekommen, geblieben, aufgestanden, eingeschlafen, geworden. Everything else takes haben.
Most verbs build the perfect with haben. sein is for movement from place to place and for changes of state — and for the three odd ones out: sein, bleiben, werden.
Movement and change of state take sein: ich bin gegangen, ich bin gefahren, ich bin geblieben. The rule is about the verb, not about you.
This verb takes haben in the perfect. sein is reserved for movement from one place to another and for changing state.
Movement and change of state take sein, so the plural is sind: wir sind gefahren, sie sind angekommen.
This verb builds the perfect with haben: wir haben gegessen, sie haben gearbeitet.
Movement and change of state take sein: du bist gekommen, du bist aufgestanden.
This verb takes haben: du hast gemacht, du hast gesehen.
Movement and change of state take sein, so ihr takes seid: ihr seid gefahren.
This verb takes haben, so ihr takes habt. Note the spelling too: seid is the verb, seit is the preposition for time.
In the past perfect the same rule applies one tense back: verbs that take sein use war, so ich war gegangen, not ich hatte gegangen.
This verb takes haben, so the past perfect uses hatte: ich hatte gegessen.
Plural past perfect of a sein-verb is waren: wir waren angekommen.
This verb takes haben, so the plural past perfect is hatten.
werden itself takes sein in the perfect: er ist Arzt geworden. wird is the present tense and is not building a perfect at all.

_: VERB ENDINGS. Keyed by the ending rather than the verb, so one entry covers every regular verb in the language.

why: du takes -st. The present endings are ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en, and they are the same for almost every verb in German.
ich takes -e. -st belongs to du only.
er, sie and es take -t, as does ihr. -e is the ich form.
ich takes -e. -t is er/sie/es and ihr.
-st is du; er, sie, es and ihr take -t.
du takes -st. -t is er/sie/es and ihr.
-en is the infinitive and the wir/sie/Sie form. A single third person, or ihr, takes -t.
wir, sie and Sie take -en — the same form as the infinitive. So does a verb pushed to the end of the clause after a modal.
-e is ich; wir, sie and Sie take -en. An infinitive after a modal is also -en.
ich takes -e. -en is wir/sie/Sie, or the infinitive.
-st is du only. wir, sie and Sie take -en, and so does an infinitive.
du takes -st. -en is the wir/sie/Sie form and the infinitive, so this is the ending you reach for when the subject slips out of sight.
du takes -st. When the stem already ends in -t, -d or -n after a consonant, an extra e goes in first: du arbeitest, du findest, du rechnest.
er, sie and es take -t. After a stem ending in -t or -d it becomes -et: er arbeitet, er findet.
ich takes -e. Dropping it is fine in casual speech and wrong in writing.
This form takes no ending — a modal verb in the ich or er/sie/es form has none: ich kann, er muss, sie will.
Modal verbs have no ending in the ich and er/sie/es forms: ich darf, er soll, sie mag.
Modal verbs take no -e in the ich form: ich kann, not ich kanne.
The extra e goes in only when the stem ends in -t, -d, or -m/-n after another consonant. Otherwise du is plain -st.
The extra e goes in only after a stem ending in -t or -d. Otherwise it is plain -t.
Strong verbs with a in the stem take an umlaut in the du and er/sie/es forms: du fährst, er fährt. The wir, ihr and sie forms do not change.
er/sie/es takes the umlaut: er fährt. ihr fahrt has no umlaut, which is why the two look confusingly alike.
Stem a and au take an umlaut in du and er/sie/es: du läufst, er läuft.
er läuft with the umlaut; ihr lauft without it.
Stem a takes an umlaut in du and er/sie/es: du schläfst, er schläft.
Stem a takes an umlaut in du and er/sie/es: du trägst, er trägt.
halten is strong: du hältst, er hält. The t of the stem and the t of the ending merge in er hält.
Strong verbs with e in the stem change it to ie or i in du and er/sie/es: du siehst, er sieht.
er sieht with ie; ihr seht keeps the plain e. Same spelling trap as fährt and fahrt.
lesen changes e to ie: du liest, er liest. The s of the stem swallows the s of the -st ending, so both forms are liest.
er liest with ie; ihr lest with plain e.
Stem e becomes i in du and er/sie/es: du sprichst, er spricht.
er spricht with i; ihr sprecht with e.
geben changes e to i: du gibst, er gibt.
er gibt with i; ihr gebt with e. es gibt — there is — uses the same form.
nehmen changes e to i and doubles the m: du nimmst, er nimmt.
er nimmt; ihr nehmt. The double m appears only in the changed forms.
essen changes e to i: du isst, er isst. ihr esst keeps the e.
helfen changes e to i: du hilfst, er hilft. It also takes the dative: ich helfe dir.
treffen changes e to i: du triffst, er trifft.
werden is irregular: ich werde, du wirst, er wird, wir werden, ihr werdet, sie werden.
wissen is irregular in the singular: ich weiß, du weißt, er weiß. The plural is regular: wir wissen.
ich weiß, not ich wisse. wissen follows the modal pattern: no ending in the ich and er/sie/es forms.
Modals change their vowel in the singular and keep it in the plural: ich kann, wir können. The infinitive is können.
Modal verbs take no ending in the ich and er/sie/es forms: ich muss, er muss.

_: NEGATION. nicht or kein is a decision English never asks you to make.

why: kein negates a noun that has ein or no article at all: ich habe kein Auto. nicht negates verbs, adjectives and everything else.
nicht negates the verb, an adjective, or a noun that carries a definite article or a possessive: das ist nicht mein Auto. kein is only for ein-nouns and bare nouns.
kein negates a noun with ein or no article, and it takes ein's endings — keine for feminine and plural.
Use nicht when the noun has der/die/das or a possessive in front of it, and for negating verbs and adjectives.
kein negates an ein-noun or a bare noun, and takes ein's endings — masculine accusative is keinen: ich habe keinen Hunger.
nicht is the negation once the noun has a definite article or a possessive.
kein in the dative is keinem for masculine and neuter, keiner for feminine, keinen for plural.
nicht negates; nichts means nothing and is a pronoun standing in for a thing. Ich esse nicht — I am not eating. Ich esse nichts — I am eating nothing.
nichts means nothing and fills a noun slot. nicht only negates.
nein answers a question. nicht negates inside a sentence — the two are never interchangeable, unlike English no and not.
Sie is the polite form and takes the plural verb: Sie sind, Sie haben, Sie kommen. Use it with strangers, officials, shopkeepers and at work until told otherwise — and it is always capitalised.
du is for friends, family, children, and anyone who has offered it. Once someone says du, switching back to Sie reads as a rebuke.
More than one person: ihr, with the -t ending. du is one person only.
mich is accusative, mir is dative. Dative after mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu, aus, and after helfen, danken, gehören, gefallen, passen and antworten.
mich is the direct object: er sieht mich. mir is the indirect object and follows the dative prepositions.
dich is accusative, dir is dative — same split as mich and mir, and the same list of dative verbs and prepositions.
dich is the direct object: ich sehe dich.
ihn is masculine accusative, ihm is masculine and neuter dative.
ihn is the direct object; ihm is the indirect one, or follows a dative preposition.

Two readings, and the key cannot tell them apart because German capitalisation does not survive here. If this was she or they: the feminine dative is ihr — ich helfe ihr, ich gebe ihr das Buch — while sie covers the nominative and the accusative. If this was the polite Sie: for several people you are on du terms with, use ihr, with the -t ending.

Two readings. If the answer is she or they: feminine nominative and accusative are both sie, while ihr is the dative — and also means her as a possessive, which is why it feels overloaded. If the answer is the polite Sie: use it for anyone you have not been offered du by, and it takes the plural verb.
er is the subject, ihn is the direct object: er sieht mich, ich sehe ihn.
The subject of the verb is er; ihn is the direct object. Whoever is doing the verb is nominative, whatever comes first in the sentence.
wir is the subject; uns is both the accusative and the dative object, and the reflexive: wir treffen uns.
ihr is the subject form; euch is the object and the reflexive: ich sehe euch, ihr trefft euch.
The reflexive changes with the person: mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich. sich is only third person and the polite Sie form.
The pronoun follows the noun's gender, not whether it is a thing: a masculine object is er or ihn, a feminine one sie. Only neuter nouns are es.
A feminine noun is sie even when it is an object — die Tür ist offen, sie ist offen. English it does not translate to es by default.
zu goes to people, shops and named buildings: zum Arzt, zur Bank, zu Anna. nach is for countries and cities without an article, and for nach Hause.
nach goes to countries and cities with no article, and in the fixed phrase nach Hause: nach Berlin, nach Italien, nach Hause. Both take the dative.
Countries that carry an article take in: in die Schweiz, in die Türkei, in die USA. Only article-less countries and cities take nach.
Cities and article-less countries take nach: nach München, nach Spanien.
in means into an enclosed space you will be inside: ins Kino, in die Stadt. zu points at a destination without entering it.
zu is the destination preposition for people and services: zum Arzt, zur Post. It always takes the dative.
mit is with, in the sense of together with or by means of. bei is at someone's place, or during. Both take the dative.
bei means at someone's home or workplace, or near: bei mir, bei Siemens, beim Bahnhof.
vor is how long ago something happened: vor drei Jahren. seit is how long something has been going on and is still going: seit drei Jahren.
seit marks a period that started in the past and continues now — and German uses the present tense with it: ich wohne seit zwei Jahren hier.
German does not use für for a stretch of time that is still going. That is seit with the present tense.
auf is on top of a horizontal surface; an is on a vertical one, or right beside it: auf dem Tisch, an der Wand.
an is against or beside — walls, doors, rivers, windows: an der Wand, am Fenster, am Rhein.
an is used for days and dates, and for being at an edge or a surface: am Montag, am 3. Mai, am Meer. in is for months, seasons, years and enclosed spaces.
in is used for months, seasons, years and enclosed spaces: im Mai, im Sommer, in der Küche. an is for days, dates and edges.
um gives clock times and nothing else: um acht Uhr. am gives days and dates: am Montag. im gives months, seasons and years: im Mai.
am is for days and dates: am Montag, am 3. Mai. um is only ever a clock time.
aus is out of an enclosed space, and where you come from originally: aus Indien, aus dem Haus. von is from a point, a person or a direction.
von is from a person, a point or a direction: von meinem Bruder, vom Bahnhof. Both take the dative.
für is for, in the sense of intended for, and it takes the accusative: für mich, für einen Freund.
über is above or across, and also about a topic. auf is directly on the surface.
bis is until or as far as. For a destination you travel to, nach or zu is the one you want.

_: CONFUSABLE WORDS. Pairs where both are real German and only one fits. `both: true` registers the reverse direction as well, because the distinction is the lesson either way round.

why: wissen is knowing a fact, and it takes a clause: ich weiß, dass... kennen is being familiar with a person, place or thing, and it takes a direct object: ich kenne Berlin.
machen is the everyday do or make and covers almost everything. tun is narrower and appears mostly in fixed phrases: es tut mir leid, was soll ich tun.
sagen is to say something — it needs content. sprechen is to speak, as an activity or a language: ich spreche Deutsch, ich sage nichts.
Both mean speak. sprechen is the neutral one and the only one for languages; reden is more about talking at length, often informally.
erzählen is to tell a story or recount something at length. sagen is a single statement.
sehen is to see — what your eyes do. schauen and gucken are to look, deliberately. Same split as see and look in English.
gehen is on foot, always. Anything with wheels or an engine is fahren, and flying is fliegen. Ich gehe nach Berlin means you are walking there.
wenn is if, or whenever something repeats. wann is the question word when, and only appears in questions or indirect questions.
wann asks a question: wann kommst du? It also survives in indirect questions: ich weiß nicht, wann er kommt.
als is for a single completed event in the past: als ich klein war. wenn is for the present, the future, or something repeated in the past.
wenn covers if, and whenever — including repeated events in the past. als is only for one specific past occasion.
ob is whether — it introduces an open question: ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt. wenn is if in the conditional sense.
Both mean because. denn is a coordinating conjunction and leaves the word order alone; weil sends the verb to the end of its clause.
weil is the usual because, and it pushes the verb to the end: weil ich müde bin.
sondern is but after a negative, correcting it: nicht heute, sondern morgen. aber is but in the sense of however.
aber is the general but. sondern only works when the first half was negated and the second half replaces it.
dass with two s is the conjunction that: ich glaube, dass er kommt. das with one s is the article or the relative pronoun. If you can swap in welches, it is das.
das with one s is the neuter article or a relative pronoun. The test: if the word could be replaced by dieses or welches, it is das.
man with one n is the impersonal one or you-in-general: man sagt. Mann with two n is a man, and is capitalised.
Mann is a noun — capital M, two n. man is the impersonal pronoun.
seit with t is the preposition for time: seit zwei Jahren. seid with d is the verb form for ihr.
seid with d is ihr seid, the verb. seit with t is since.
war is the past tense of sein. wahr with an h means true.
viel is much or a lot, and quantifies a noun or an action. sehr is very, and intensifies an adjective or an adverb: sehr gut, viel Arbeit, ich arbeite viel.
In comparisons, als is used for differences — größer als. wie is used for equality — so groß wie.
wie goes with so...wie for things that are equal: so groß wie ich. als is for a comparative that says one is more than the other.
noch is still, or yet to come. schon is already. Ich bin noch hier — still here. Ich bin schon hier — already here.
erst means only or not until, and frames the amount as small or the time as late. schon frames it as large or early. Er ist erst zwei — only two. Er ist schon zwei — already two.
erst is only in the sense of not yet more, with an implication that more will come. nur is only as a plain limit.
immer is always, without exception. oft is often. German does not soften immer the way English softens always.
legen is to lay something down and takes an object and the accusative. liegen is to be lying there, takes no object and the dative. The pattern repeats: stellen/stehen, setzen/sitzen.
stellen is to put something upright, with an object and the accusative. stehen is to be standing, no object, dative.
setzen is to place or seat, with an object and the accusative. sitzen is to be sitting, no object, dative.
studieren is to study at university, as a degree. Learning a language or revising for school is lernen.
bekommen is to get or receive — a false friend for become. werden is to become.
werden builds the future and means become. wollen means want to — a false friend for will.
groß is big, and is the word for a person's height. hoch is high off the ground — buildings, mountains, prices.
kalt is cold. kühl is cool — pleasant or mildly chilly, never freezing.
Zeit is time as a substance: ich habe keine Zeit. Mal is an occasion you can count: dreimal, das nächste Mal.
Uhr is the clock and the o'clock in a time: um acht Uhr. Stunde is an hour as a duration: zwei Stunden.
Stelle is a specific job or position you can apply for. Arbeit is work in general, and Beruf is the profession you trained in.
möchte is would like — a polite request. mögen is to like in general: ich mag Kaffee, ich möchte einen Kaffee.
dürfen is to be allowed to; können is to be able to. German keeps the two apart where English says can for both.
müssen is must — a real necessity. sollen is should, or being told to by somebody else.
brauchen is to need something, with an object. müssen is must, with a verb. And nicht brauchen zu, not nicht müssen, is the usual way to say need not.
heißen is to be called: ich heiße Anna. nennen is to call something something else, and takes two objects.
wohnen is to live at an address. leben is to be alive, or to live in a broader sense — in a country, in an era.
fragen is to ask a question. bitten is to ask for something, and takes um: ich bitte um Hilfe.
warten is to wait, and takes auf plus the accusative. erwarten is to expect, and takes a plain object.
Both express liking, but the grammar flips: ich mag den Film, but der Film gefällt mir — the thing is the subject and you are in the dative.
lieber is the comparative of gern and means prefer to do: ich trinke lieber Tee. besser is the comparative of gut and means better in quality.
nächste is next in a sequence. andere is other or different, with no order implied.
Leute is people in the everyday sense and has no singular. Menschen is human beings, more formal or more literal.
schnell means fast. German fast means almost — a false friend that changes the sentence completely.
fast means almost; bald means soon. Neither means the English fast.
eventuell means possibly, not eventually. For eventually, use schließlich or am Ende.
aktuell means current or up to date, not actual. For actually, use tatsächlich or eigentlich.
sensibel means sensitive. Sensible is vernünftig.
Chef is the boss. A chef who cooks is a Koch.
Gift means poison. A present is a Geschenk.
auch means also. German also means so or therefore.
Rat is advice. The animal is a Ratte.
In German, Handy is a mobile phone. For handy in the English sense, use praktisch.

_: STRUCTURAL. Keyed by shape rather than by word, so they fire whenever the same words come out in the wrong order — or the right word comes out in the wrong case.

why: In a main clause the conjugated verb is always the second element — not the second word, the second unit. Put anything you like first, a time, a place, an object, and the verb still comes next, with the subject after it: Heute gehe ich ins Kino.

German word order is freer than English about what comes first and much stricter about the verb. Inside the rest of the clause the order is time, then manner, then place: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Köln.
Every noun in German is capitalised, wherever it appears in the sentence. So are Sie and Ihr in the polite form. Everything else, including ich and adjectives of nationality, is lower case.

An umlaut or an ß is not decoration — it changes the word. schon and schön, Mutter and Mütter, and in the plural of many nouns the umlaut is the only thing marking it. If you cannot type them, ae, oe, ue and ss are the accepted substitutes.

_: LAST RESORT, one per tag. These fire when nothing more specific matches, and they exist so the offline and no-key paths give a rule rather than a label.

why: The article is part of the word. There are useful endings — -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tion and -in are feminine, -chen and -lein are neuter, -er and -ling are usually masculine — but the reliable method is to learn every noun with its article from the first time you see it.

The accusative marks the direct object. Only masculine changes: der becomes den, ein becomes einen, kein becomes keinen, mein becomes meinen. Feminine, neuter and plural look identical to the nominative.
The dative marks the indirect object and follows mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu, aus, außer and gegenüber. der and das become dem, die becomes der, plural die becomes den and the noun gains an -n.
The genitive shows possession: masculine and neuter take des with an -s on the noun, feminine and plural take der. In speech it is mostly replaced by von plus the dative.
The present endings are ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en. They are the same for nearly every verb; strong verbs change the stem vowel in the du and er/sie/es forms as well.
The conjugated verb is the second element of a main clause, whatever comes first. After weil, dass, wenn, ob, als and every other subordinating conjunction it goes to the very end instead.
After a modal — können, müssen, wollen, sollen, dürfen, mögen — the second verb goes to the end of the clause as a plain infinitive: Ich muss heute früh nach Hause gehen.
German has five plural patterns — -e, -er, -n/-en, -s, and no ending at all — often with an umlaut. Learn the plural with the word, the same way you learn the article.
kein negates a noun that has ein or no article; nicht negates everything else. nicht normally goes at the end of the clause, but before an adjective, a place phrase or a separable prefix.
Pronouns change with case: ich/mich/mir, du/dich/dir, er/ihn/ihm, sie/sie/ihr, wir/uns/uns, ihr/euch/euch, sie/sie/ihnen. And du, ihr and Sie are three different people to be talking to.
Every noun is capitalised in German, and so are Sie and Ihr in the polite form. Nothing else is.
Umlauts and ß carry meaning; ae, oe, ue and ss are the accepted substitutes if you cannot type them. Watch das/dass, seit/seid and man/Mann, where one letter changes the grammar.
The verb is second in a main clause and last in a subordinate one. In between, the order is time, then manner, then place.

A different word was needed here. German splits several English words in two — know into wissen and kennen, go into gehen and fahren, put into legen, stellen and setzen — so a direct translation often lands on the wrong one.

Prepositions do not map one to one between languages, and each one fixes a case. Dative always: mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu, aus. Accusative always: für, um, durch, gegen, ohne, bis. Two-way, dative for where and accusative for where to: in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen.

The perfect uses haben for most verbs and sein for verbs of movement from one place to another and of changing state — plus sein, bleiben and werden themselves. It is a property of the verb, so it can be learned once per verb.
